Acids Acids
There are four strong acids in common use: Oil of Vitriol, Aqua Fortis, Spirit of Salt, and Aqua Regis. The first three must be stored in special glass bottles. While Aqua Regia must be used immediately once it is made as it constantly gives off gas and the pressure of these gases will destroy any container that is capable of holding it.
Acids may be either thrown, or poured into a solution or over an item (such as a chain, or a door lock).
AcidsPouring When pouring acid a single crafting check is made when opening the vial. If the acid has been created by a PC using the Alchemy ability then the check is made using that characters Alchemy Craft check. If the acid has been made by an NPC then the player makes a check for the NPC creator at Rank 0. A fail represents poor quality acid that is weak the GM can determine the effect of the reduced strength acid. Critical fails have different effects described for each type of acid.
AcidsThrowing When throwing acid a two checks are made. The first is a Throw Object check to see where the object lands, the second is a crafting check with results dependent on the type of acid.
AcidsBroken Vial If some mishap causes a vial of acid to break on the characters person then 1d4 random colocated items are also destroyed and possibly the PC suffers acid damage as well.

Falling Damage
When a character falls the type of damage they receive depends on how far they fall, see Table table:falling on page table:falling-table. The GM should feel free to make allowances for the character slowing their fall, or the surface that the character is landing on as they see fit. For example the characters should be allowed to make a Luck check to see if they fall on something soft or at least not to damaging or perhaps hitting an awning half way down. The characters could make an agility check to see if they are able to grab something to reduce the speed of their fall. Each such success should reduce the fall damage by one tier in the Falling Damage table.
For example, a character falls off the top of a five story building. They make an agility check and hit an awning on the way down. They make a further Luck check and land in a stack of hay.

Suffocation and Drowning
Most people can hold their breath for 2 minutes, 12 combat rounds. Beyond that they must start to roll on the Near Death table. Once they can breathe again then they are restored completely. No hit points are lost. If they rolled a bane on any of their death rolls the GM might consider giving them an aspect or a temporary condition.

Insanitysec:insanity
When under stress or in the face of great danger a character might succumb to insanity. See the section on Insanities below. Insanity might at the GMs discretion lead to sudden insights or vice versa.
Generally new Aspects for a character are chosen cooperatively by the party with the intent to generate interesting social dynamics within the game. Madnesses are a type of aspect that are imposed upon the player by the GM. While aspects are generally a two edged sword, madnesses are usually a curse.

Aflictions Afflictions
Afflictions are similar to aspects but are used to model physical debilities, infirmaties, afflictions, insanities, and diseases, while Aspects are used to model more mental and mind set related traits.

Transmission. - Injury, Contact, Ingested, and Inhaled.
Airborne : Tiny droplet nuclei or dust stay in the air for a long time and travel far on air currents. Examples include measles and tuberculosis.Fomites (surfaces): Germs live on non-living objects like doorknobs, phones, or toys until touched by a new host. Examples include norovirus and the common cold.Vehicles: Contaminated food, water, or blood products carry pathogens to multiple people. Examples include cholera and hepatitis A. Vectors: Living creatures—mostly insects like mosquitoes, ticks, and fleas—carry pathogens between hosts. Examples include malaria and Lyme disease.
